name: Fletcherism

lead: Fletcherism is a chewing regimen devised by the American Horace Fletcher (1849-1919), nicknamed 'The Great Masticator.' Followers chew each mouthful until it turns to liquid, sometimes up to 100 times, and swallow only what happens on its own. Fletcher said it let him eat less, stay slimmer and stronger, and feel young again.

The appearance link is weight control and vitality: slower eating is meant to prevent overeating and improve digestion. A 2011 experiment found that 35 chews per mouthful reduced intake compared with 10 chews in a small sample, which the authors said partly confirmed Fletcher's idea.

paras: Practitioners eat only when hungry, chew each bite to a liquid, and sip drinks slowly. Fletcher also promoted a low-protein diet. Modern descriptions of mindful or slow chewing for portion control are sometimes linked back to his teachings.

Chewing itself is low-risk, but contemporaries such as Carl Malmberg and Morris Fishbein criticized the near-liquid, low-bulk diet and Fletcher's wider curative claims. Eating very slowly for long periods can interfere with social meals.

angle.text: Fletcherism was marketed as a way to eat less and stay trim and energetic by chewing thoroughly. A 2011 study of 35 versus 10 chews found reduced intake with more chewing.

lead: Fletcherism is a food-chewing doctrine promoted from about 1895 until 1919 by Horace Fletcher, a wealthy American businessman, writer and self-taught nutritionist. Followers chewed each mouthful until it liquefied, and Fletcher said the habit prevented overeating, improved digestion and strength, and helped him reduce his weight.[1][2]

The doctrine has an appearance angle: eating less, slower and with better digestion was presented as a path to a lean, energetic body, and Fletcher's 1913 book was titled 'Fletcherism: What It Is; Or, How I Became Young at Sixty.'[2] Reported adherents included Henry James and Upton Sinclair, and Yale researchers tested his method.[2][3]

Modern researchers have revisited the idea. A 2011 experiment in the journal Appetite compared 35 and 10 chews per mouthful and found higher chewing counts reduced food intake, though the sample was small.[4] Historians have also traced its influence on the food policies of Herbert Hoover during World War I.[5]
infobox: Chew food to a liquid; sip drinks slowly

paras: Fletcher was born on August 10, 1849 in Lawrence, Massachusetts, and worked as an artist, importer, opera manager and writer before devising his method to address dyspepsia and obesity.[2] He lived in Venice and died in Copenhagen on January 13, 1919. His books include Menticulture (1896) and the 1913 Fletcherism volume.[2][1]

He lectured and wrote for roughly 24 years, and the practice became known as 'Fletcherizing.'[1] Notable people who tried it included Henry James, Upton Sinclair and John D. Rockefeller; Mark Twain visited his home.[2] Fletcher was also involved with relief work in Belgium during the First World War.[2][5]

Fletcher held that food should be chewed until liquefied, and that liquids should be mixed with saliva. He advised eating only when truly hungry, not when angry or sad.[2] He claimed the method raised strength while lowering intake and could help conditions from colitis to alcoholism.[2] A historical biography notes his belief that prolonged chewing prevented overeating and improved dental and systemic health.[1]

Yale's Russell Chittenden studied the system and William Gilbert Anderson of the Yale Gymnasium tested Fletcher; Fletcher said he outperformed college athletes at 58, though the accuracy of the tests is uncertain.[2][3] Medical contemporaries called him a food faddist, and Carl Malmberg and Morris Fishbein criticized the low-bulk diet as risking constipation and intoxication.[2][3] A 1910 dental-journal article discussed some effects of Fletcherism on nutrition.[6]

A 2011 comparison of 35 versus 10 chews per mouthful, using electromyography to monitor chewing, found that higher chewing counts reduced food intake despite faster chewing, and doubled meal duration to reach 'comfortably full'; the authors noted the low sample size and called the results preliminary support for Fletcher's doctrine.[4]
